title: Phoenician Colonies
capsule: Between roughly 900 and 600 BCE, Phoenician city-states—principally Tyre and Sidon—planted a network of commercial colonies across the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, from Kition on Cyprus and Lixus on the Moroccan Atlantic to Carthage (traditionally founded 814 BCE) and Gadir (Cádiz, traditionally 1104 BCE but archaeologically confirmed by the ninth century). These colonies functioned as trading emporia for purple dye, silver, tin, and slaves rather than agricultural settlements, connected by Phoenician maritime expertise and the commercial hegemony of Tyre under kings such as Ithobaal I. By the late seventh century Assyrian domination of the Levantine homeland compressed Tyrian power, accelerating Carthage's rise as an independent western successor. The colonial network represents the broadest commercial reach of any Near Eastern Bronze-to-Iron Age polity.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The locations of major Phoenician colonies are well established archaeologically, but the precise territorial control each colony exercised and the exact chronology of founding dates remain matters of active scholarly debate.
